heading: What a Conceptual Data Model Is (and Why ER)
title: Real-world things → their ER element (not tables yet)
rows: not a PRIMARY KEY clause yet
note: The conceptual (ER) model captures WHAT data exists using real-world things and symbols — tables, columns and foreign keys (the HOW) come later in S12. It is technology-neutral, so a registrar or finance manager can verify it.

heading: The Database Design Process
title: The four design stages (RCLP) worked on eSewa
rows: store users & transactions; must send money, show statement
'top-up source' never captured → painful live migration
USER —MAKES— TRANSACTION drawn as a diamond
jump to tables → rewrite when 'one user, many wallets' appears
ER mapped to relational tables + keys
User & Transaction tables + a user_id foreign key
wrong keys → duplicate or orphaned rows
an index on transaction date so the statement loads in a tap
the statement screen crawls at month-end
note: Each stage feeds the next; ER sits at the conceptual stage, ER→tables is the logical stage. Every stage you skip, a later stage pays for — with interest. Mirrors Unit 1's conceptual → logical → internal schema levels.

heading: Data vs Functional Requirements
title: Sort each Khalti requirement: data (noun) or functional (verb)?
headers: What it shapes in the design
rows: Store each user's name, number, KYC
Record every transaction's amount, date, status
an operation the design must serve
Top up from a linked bank
View statement for a date range
operation → drives an index on date
note: Data requirements (nouns) become entities & attributes; functional requirements (verbs) are the operations the design must serve. Capture BOTH — store the right data yet miss the verbs and you ship a correct but painfully slow system.

heading: Entity, Entity Type, Entity Set
title: Entity vs entity type vs entity set across Nepali systems
note: The TYPE is the stable category (design-time, a rectangle); the SET changes every second as things come and go; an ENTITY is one member. One type → many sets, exactly like one schema → many instances (S2).

heading: Attributes and Their Four Types
title: The four attribute types (+ key) with Chen symbol and mapping
headers: How it maps to tables later (S12)
rows: age from DOB; order total; loan balance
a customer's phone numbers; Daraz saved addresses
breaks out into its OWN table
note: Classify attributes now and table design falls out later: multivalued → own table, composite → split columns, derived → never stored, key → primary key. Storing a derived value (e.g. age) causes update anomalies — it rots every birthday.

heading: Keys
title: Good keys vs bad 'keys' — and why they fail
note: Test any proposed key: could two different real things ever share this value, or could it change? Names, emails and phones fail — national IDs, roll numbers and system IDs are designed to be unique, stable and minimal.

heading: Relationship Type, Set & Degree
title: Relationships across Nepali systems: type, degree, one pair
headers: A pair in its set right now
note: A relationship is a real-world association (a diamond), not a foreign key. Its TYPE is the named verb, its SET is today's pairings, its DEGREE is how many entity types the verb joins (2 = binary, the common case).

heading: Roles & Recursive (Self) Relationships
title: Recursive relationships — the two roles you must name
note: In a recursive (self) relationship the same entity type sits on both ends, so role names are MANDATORY — without them the direction (who supervises / mentors / invited whom) is simply lost.

heading: Cardinality Ratio (1:1, 1:N, M:N)
title: 1:1, 1:N, M:N — read both ways, then map
rows: one citizen ↔ at most one passport, and back
one dept has many staff; each staff one dept
one user many txns; each txn one user
many products per order; many orders per product
note: Find the ratio by checking the MAXIMUM on each side (read it both ways). 1:N becomes a foreign key on the 'many' side; every M:N must break out into a junction table when mapped — it has no single 'other side' to point to.

heading: Participation (Total vs Partial)
title: Total vs partial participation — each side, each line
rows: no loan may exist without a customer
a customer may have zero loans
every transaction belongs to a user
a brand-new user may have zero txns
every installment is tied to a loan
note: Participation is the MINIMUM (whether at all); cardinality is the maximum (how many) — they are independent. Total = double line = must participate; partial = single line = optional. Making a mandatory side partial allows orphan records — an audit disaster.

heading: Weak vs Strong (Regular) Entity Types
title: Strong vs weak entities — own key or borrowed identity?
rows: two staff can each have a child 'Ram'
a reply has no identity without its post
note: 'Weak' means IDENTITY-DEPENDENT (no key of its own), never unimportant — order items, loan installments and exam answer-sheets are business-critical. A strong entity is a single rectangle; a weak entity a double rectangle.

heading: The Identifying (Owner) Relationship
title: Weak entity + owner + identifying (double-diamond) link
note: The identifying relationship (a DOUBLE diamond) supplies the identity a weak entity lacks, and the weak side is ALWAYS total participation (double line). Examiners look for the 'three doubles': double rectangle + double diamond + double line.

heading: The Partial Key (Discriminator)
title: Partial key + owner key = the full identifier
rows: same seq exists on other posts
note: A partial key is unique only WITHIN one owner (dashed underline). Full identity = owner's primary key + partial key — exactly the S6 composite-key idea. The partial key alone always collides across owners.
